title: Shaking Off the Dust
english: … set free from every stain. For we have been justified through faith in him, and we have been enriched with the security he gives against anything at all. We are walled about, as it were, by his grace, since he drives away from us every assault of the devil and the savage uprisings of the opposing powers.

He teaches this when he speaks to Zion, that is, to Jerusalem, which is “the Church of the living God” (1 Timothy 3:15): “The uncircumcised and unclean will no longer pass through you again” (Isaiah 52:1).

Taken historically, you will understand the saying in this way. The nations living around Jerusalem may be taken as the uncircumcised and unclean, since they neither knew the One who is God by nature and in truth nor had received the training that comes through the Law. They fought very often against those of Israel’s blood, so that in most places they were seen to be stronger than the strength Israel had, and they all but walked through Jerusalem, holding her thrown down under their feet.

Come, then, let us shape the spiritual meaning from what at times happened in history. The troops of demons, that is, “the world rulers of this darkness” (Ephesians 6:12), and with them the profane Satan, hold under their feet the souls that have not yet come under God. They pass through them, as it were, with no one to stop them, that is, no one to come to their defense. But when those souls have been made God’s own and have him as their glory and strength, then, yes then, the greed of those powers will come to an end. For it is written: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will rescue them” (Psalm 34:7).
So the uncircumcised and unclean may be understood as the loathsome and profane powers that produce every kind of filth, the wicked and opposing powers.
“Shake off the dust, and rise up, and sit down, Jerusalem. Loose the bond from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” (Isaiah 52:2).

He now shows her to be skilled in boasts fit for saints, and he teaches plainly how she will put on the strength of her arm and her glory as well (compare Isaiah 51:9; 52:1). First he commands her to shake off the dust, and so to rise and sit, and to take off the bond from her neck. Here, I think, the dust should be understood as the earthly mind and the uncleanness of fleshly desires.

For just as those who lie on the ground cannot help being covered with dust and dirt, so in the same way, I think, the thoughts of fleshly uncleanness settle on those whose mind is thrown to the ground and whose outlook is earthly. So we who have been called into spiritual kinship with our Lord Jesus Christ, and who are about to put him on as strength and glory (compare Romans 13:14), must first shake off the dusty, earthly mind and first cleanse the mind, and …
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Commentary on Isaiah (CPG 5203). The section opens mid-word (…ης κηλῖδος) and ends after καὶ προκαθᾶραι τὸν νοῦν, κ…; both breaks are marked with an ellipsis and nothing is filled in.
τὰς οὔπω γεγενημένας ὑπὸ Θεῷ ψυχάς: ‘souls that have not yet come under God’ (ὑπό with the dative), not ‘souls not yet begotten by God’.
Psalm 34:7 is Psalm 33:8 in the Septuagint. ‘The strength of her arm’ echoes Isaiah 51:9 (ἔνδυσαι τὴν ἰσχὺν τοῦ βραχίονός σου) and ‘glory’ Isaiah 52:1.

title: He Suffered for Us All
english: … so that, as Paul says, he might sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). For he suffered not for himself (far from it) but for the whole world under heaven.

The all-wise Paul will bear witness, writing of God the Father: “He did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all, so that with him he might also give us all things” (Romans 8:32). And the Son himself says somewhere, through the lyre of the Psalmist, to his Father and God in heaven: “Sacrifice and offering you did not want, but a body you prepared for me. In whole burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure. Then I said, ‘Here I am, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me.’ To do your will, O God, I have desired” (Psalm 40:6–8; compare Hebrews 10:5–7).

The worship under the Law was of no use to those on earth for taking away sin, since the sacrifices of oxen and the slaughter of sheep were not what God wanted. So the true Lamb, “who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), offered himself for us “as a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians 5:2). Then, having endured death in the flesh, he set the whole world under heaven free from both death and sin. For One who outweighs all in worth suffered for all, so that he might rule and reign over all.

Paul will confirm this again when he writes: “For this reason Christ died and lived, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living” (Romans 14:9). And again: “One died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15).

Rightly, then, the prophet says: “This man, who was under the blow, who knew how to bear sickness, whose face was turned away, who was dishonored and not esteemed, bears our sins and suffers pain for us; and we reckoned him to be in toil, under a blow, and in affliction” (Isaiah 53:3–4).

Look again, I ask you, with what skill the prophetic word moves forward here. It takes on the part of those who did not know the mystery of Christ, and who thought that he came to suffer as one paying for his own sins. “For we reckoned him to be in toil, under a blow, and in affliction,” he says; that is, we supposed that the suffering had come upon him from God, as if for some sins, and that he was in toil, under a blow, and in affliction because of that sin.

But it is not so at all; rather, “he was wounded because of our sins, and made weak because of our lawless deeds” (Isaiah 53:5). Then he gives further reasons, through which one can see that he “who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21) came to suffer for the sake of our salvation and life.
For long ago we stood apart from God in enmity, fighting against his holy laws, not bearing the yoke of obedience, and refusing to serve him. But it was necessary …
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Commentary on Isaiah (CPG 5203). The section opens on a broken word (…αθεν, almost certainly ἔπαθεν, ‘he suffered’, from Hebrews 13:12); it is not translated and is marked with an ellipsis. The section ends mid-word (ἀναγκαῖο…).
Psalm 40:6–8 is Psalm 39:7–9 in the Septuagint; Cyril’s ‘a body you prepared for me’ is the Septuagint wording also quoted in Hebrews 10:5–7.
Romans 8:32 is a question in Paul (‘how will he not also give us all things?’); Cyril recasts it as a purpose clause, and the English follows Cyril.
ὡς ἰδίων ἁμαρτημάτων ἀποστήσων: the participle is odd (perhaps for ἀποτίσων, ‘paying for’); rendered by the sense the next sentence makes plain, ‘as one paying for his own sins’.
Isaiah 53:5 in the Septuagint has ‘wounded because of our lawless deeds, made weak because of our sins’; Cyril has the two nouns the other way round, and the English follows Cyril.

title: Idols Under the Leafy Trees
english: … the One who would set you in order for godliness through the commands of the Gospel.

“You who urge others on to the idols under leafy trees, slaughtering their children in the ravines among the rocks: that is your portion, this is your lot. To them you poured out drink offerings, and to them you offered up sacrifices. Shall I not be angry at these things? On a high and lofty mountain, there is your bed, and there you brought up sacrifices; and behind the posts of your door you set your memorial” (Isaiah 57:5–8).

Having shown them to be killers of the Lord, he shows that their God-hating sickness and their readiness for bloodshed were nothing new in them, but had been in them for a long time, from of old. “For you are the ones,” he says, “who in the times of old urged others on to the idols under leafy trees.”

The Law given through Moses awarded them what was good for them and said plainly, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10; compare Deuteronomy 6:13). Yet they slid into such madness, or rather into a godlessness unrestrained and beyond all measure, that they became makers of idols, offered sacrifice to them, and urged others, that is, taught them, to worship under leafy trees and to crown the idols with honors fit only for God.

The God of all makes this plain through the voice of Jeremiah, saying: “Have you seen what the house of Israel has done to me? They went up on every high mountain and under every leafy tree, and there they prostituted themselves” (Jeremiah 3:6). For they took over the mountain peaks and the most flowering parts of the groves, built altars and sacred precincts, and brought sacrifices and drink offerings there to the unclean demons. And there were some who did not spare even their own children. Jechonias, indeed, slaughtered his own son to gods that do not exist.
God himself said this somewhere through one of the holy prophets, exposing the cruelty of those who were used to doing such things: “Sacrifice human beings, for the calves have run out” (Hosea 13:2).

“You, then,” he says, “are the ones who urge others on to the idols, slaughtering their children under leafy trees in the ravines among the rocks.” What then follows? “That is your portion, this is your lot.” “You have worshiped empty things,” he says, “and you will have a portion like them, and your lot will be empty.”

Or perhaps he means this: “You slaughtered their children in the ravines,” he says. “So that is your portion, this is your lot”; that is, you will be caught in the same evils, and slaughter will become your portion and lot. For what reason? First, because you became a killer of children; then, because you poured out drink offerings to unclean demons and lifeless idols, and offered up sacrifices to them. So then, at these things shall I not be angry …
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Commentary on Isaiah (CPG 5203). The section opens on a broken verb (…έχεσθε, perhaps ἀνέχεσθε, ‘you bear with’); the verb is not supplied, and the English keeps only the object phrase after an ellipsis. The section ends mid-word (ὀργισθ…).
παρακαλοῦντες ἐπὶ τὰ εἴδωλα: Cyril himself glosses παρακαλεῖν as ‘teach others’, so the lemma is rendered ‘urge others on to the idols’.
Κυριοκτόνους (‘killers of the Lord’) is Cyril’s polemical charge against the people addressed; it is translated as written.
‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ is the wording of Matthew 4:10 (and Luke 4:8); Deuteronomy 6:13 in the Septuagint reads ‘fear’ and lacks ‘alone’.
Jechonias is the Septuagint form of Jeconiah; Scripture records child sacrifice by Ahaz and Manasseh (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6), so the name is Cyril’s and is kept.
